content: Equisetum arvense, commonly known as the Field Horsetail, is a perennial plant characterized by its bushy appearance and rhizomatous stem structure. It is native to the northern hemisphere. This plant produces two types of stems: sterile and fertile. The sterile stems emerge after the fertile stems have withered. These sterile stems are typically taller and bushier, with jointed segments that are approximately one inch in length and about 1/20th of an inch in diameter. Each segment contains a single set of slender, erect, whorled branches. Some stems can grow up to 20 segments and reach heights of 2 to 24 inches. In contrast, the fertile stems are generally half the height of the sterile stems and are more succulent in texture. Notably, Equisetum arvense has an exceptionally high diploid chromosome number of 216 (108 pairs), which is approximately five times greater than the human diploid number of 46. This plant contains several bioactive compounds with medicinal properties. It is particularly rich in minerals such as silicon (10%), potassium, and calcium, which contribute to its diuretic effects. Equisetum arvense is often prescribed for the care of connective tissues, including cartilage, tendons, and bones. It is also used to manage conditions such as polyps, epistaxis (nosebleeds), and other forms of bleeding. In Japan, the buds of this plant are consumed as a vegetable during the spring season. Historically, it was used to polish pewter and wood, earning it the name pewterwort, and was also employed to strengthen fingernails. In herbal medicine, Equisetum arvense has been used to treat kidney and bladder disorders, gastroenteritis, and infections of the prostate and urinary tract. When applied externally, it has been used to manage chilblains and wounds.
